title: Mother, grandfather, uncle
hook: his mother dies when he is six, his grandfather two years later, and each time someone takes him in

segments.voice: Yesterday, yatim: the orphan nobody wanted, and Halimah, who took him anyway. Your line was Allah shelters the orphan.

He comes back from the desert a little boy, sunburned, speaking Bedouin Arabic, and goes home to his mother, Aminah. For a short while, it's the two of them. When he's six, she takes him north to the town of Yathrib, to see relatives and visit the grave of the father he never met. With them on the long camel ride: a servant woman named Umm Ayman. On the way home, at a place called al-Abwa', Aminah falls ill. She dies there, on the road. A six-year-old boy stands by his mother's grave in the desert, a long way from home.
screen: `HOME TO HIS MOTHER.` → `A TRIP TO HIS FATHER'S GRAVE.` → `AT AL-ABWA', SHE DIES.`

segments.voice: Umm Ayman brings him back to Mecca, and someone takes him in: his grandfather, 'Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief from the elephant story. Ibn Ishaq's biography has a tender detail. The old man had a rug laid out in the shade of the Ka'ba, and none of his grown sons would dare sit on it, out of respect. The little boy would climb right onto it, and when his uncles tried to move him, the old man said: leave him be. Two years later, when the boy is eight, his grandfather dies too. Again someone takes him in: his uncle Abu Talib, a man with many children and not much money, who raises him as his own and will protect him for the rest of his life. Three homes by the age of eight. And through all of it, Umm Ayman stayed; he is reported to have called her his mother after his mother. He never forgot Aminah. A hadith in Sahih Muslim tells how, as a grown man, the Prophet ﷺ visited her grave and wept, and everyone around him wept too. This is part of why Islam speaks of parents and caregivers the way it does. The Qur'an asks believers to be gentle with them as they grow old, and gives a prayer for them, in Pickthall's words: “My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.” Loss after loss, and each time, somebody opened a door.
screen: `GRANDFATHER: LEAVE HIM BE.` · `UNCLE ABU TALIB TAKES HIM IN.` · `UMM AYMAN, THROUGH ALL OF IT.` · `A GROWN MAN WEEPS AT HER GRAVE.` · then, large: `SOMEONE ALWAYS TOOK HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who took you in, a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor, and picture one as they were when they looked after you. Say thank you silently, and mean it, even if they've died. If you pray, you can use the Qur'an's words: my Lord, have mercy on them both, as they cared for me when I was little.
Mother. Umm, in Arabic. Aminah, who died on the road when her son was six, and whose grave he wept at as a grown man.
Your line: someone always took him in. Tomorrow, the town starts trusting him with everything. Day eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: Honoring parents is one of the strongest duties in Islam, second in the Qur'an only to worshiping Allah; many Muslims say the prayer of 17:24 for their parents after their daily prayers.

fork.setup: you're 'Abd al-Muttalib. your little orphaned grandson has climbed onto the rug by the Ka'ba that none of your grown sons dare to sit on. his uncles move to pull him off. what do you say?
fork.reveal: Ibn Ishaq says the old man told them to leave him be, and patted his back.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad childhood.
what it means: three deaths by the age of eight, and each time someone opened a door, and he never forgot them.
what a scholar hears: al-Abwa' lies between Mecca and Medina; Umm Ayman, Barakah, was an Abyssinian servant he later freed and honored all his life.
